title: Records in the Frontend Without Extbase

hints.text: A table of your own is a TCA file and nothing else: Configuration/TCA/<table>.php declares it and the schema is derived from those columns. Reading its records on a page needs no model, no repository and no controller — that is what a data processor is for, and Extbase enters the picture when pagination, search, validated arguments or forms do.

hints: The chain is configured as dataProcessing on the PAGEVIEW or on lib.contentElement: database-query with table, pidInList or uidInList and orderBy, and a nested dataProcessing of its own. record-transformation there turns the rows into record objects, files resolves the references of an image field, and comma-separated-value parses a text field that carries a table.

List and detail can be the same page. Fill the list variable unconditionally, fill the single record only when the request carries the argument — if.isTrue.data = GP:<argument> on that processor — and let the template branch on whether it is there. uidInList.data = GP:<argument> is safe on its own: the select is built by ContentObjectRenderer, which runs uidInList through GeneralUtility::intExplode() before it reaches the query.
How such a page is addressed is record-routing, and what its title comes from is record-page-title.

hints.text: The site set ships the routing for it, in route-enhancers.yaml next to config.yaml. A detail view of that shape is a Simple enhancer whose routePath carries the argument, with a PersistedAliasMapper aspect naming the table and the slug field. The mapper's direction matters: link generation receives the record uid as the query argument and replaces it with routeFieldName in the path; route matching looks that field value up and hands the uid to the application. Thus ?record=<uid> becomes /detail/<route-field-value> — do not pass the route-field value as the query argument or validate it there.

Make routeFieldName a TCA slug with eval uniqueInSite so the reverse lookup is unambiguous within the current site. A path value for which the mapper finds no visible record rejects the enhanced route before rendering, so the record lookup is the input validation; load the selected record by the resolved uid rather than trusting display data from the request.

An argument that an enhancer maps through a static aspect — including PersistedAliasMapper and StaticValueMapper — is a routing argument and needs no cHash: the mapper restricts it to a finite or persisted set and PageArguments keeps it out of dynamicArguments. An argument left in the query string is dynamic and does need the hash on a cacheable page, so each value gets its own page-cache variant instead of reusing the first response.

limitToPages takes an Expression Language string as well as a page uid, evaluated with page, site and siteLanguage — so an enhancer can be bound to every page of one backend layout instead of to a uid. That is what makes routing shippable at all: a set is installed into installations whose page ids nobody knows in advance, and of a site configuration shipped in Initialisation/Site/ only rootPageId is remapped on import.
Advertising those addresses is a second configuration and a second selection: record-xml-sitemap is what the XML sitemap of the same table needs, and it is where the two filters drift apart.

title: An XML Sitemap of a Record Table
hints: A record table is put into the XML sitemap under plugin.tx_seo.config.xmlSitemap.sitemaps.<key>, with provider RecordsXmlSitemapDataProvider and a config block naming the table. The rows come from pid, recursive and additionalWhere; the address of each comes from url.pageId and the url.additionalGetParameters or url.fieldToParameterMap that carry the record into it.

Every address is built from that one pageId. RecordsXmlSitemapDataProvider::defineUrl() reads url.pageId once per row and falls back to the page the sitemap was requested on, so a records sitemap can only carry rows that this single page renders. Where the detail view sits on several filtered pages, the sitemap advertises all of them from one of them.

Nothing verifies the pair. The provider builds the address out of a page id it never asks about, and a page handed an argument it has no plugin for renders its own content and answers HTTP 200 — so the whole sitemap can be green and carry no record at all. What proves it is one request per sample address, read for whether the record is in the body rather than for the status.

additionalWhere is the only lever that narrows the rows, and it defaults to nothing. That means the selection is written twice — once here and once in the plugin that renders the page — and the two drift apart silently: a provider given hidden=0 alone lists every row the plugin's own filter leaves out.

What the query does apply is the deleted, hidden and start/stop restrictions, because getRestrictions()->add() adds the workspace one to the default container rather than replacing it — two sessions read that line as the whole restriction set and restated the visibility rules in additionalWhere for nothing. What is absent is the frontend group restriction, and there is no translation overlay: the language field is constrained to -1 and the current language, so a record only an fe_group may see is advertised to everybody.
This is the sitemap side of a detail view. How the record reaches the page at all is record-routing, and what the page is called once it is there is record-page-title.

hints.text: The sitemap arrives with the site set typo3/seo-sitemap. Requiring typo3/cms-seo installs the extension and leaves /sitemap.xml answering HTTP 404 until a set of the site depends on that one, which is what brings the TypoScript declaring page type 1533906435.

That set ships the routing with it: a PageType enhancer mapping sitemap.xml onto that type, and the Sitemap enhancer whose StaticValueMapper carries the sitemap name in the path. A table of your own is added as one entry to that map, which merges into the enhancer the set declares rather than replacing it.

hints: url.pageId is read as config['url']['pageId'] ?? the requested page, so a value of 0 is not a fallback. A site setting whose default is 0 — the idiomatic "nothing chosen" — is taken as page zero and every address it builds is broken, and the null coalescing is what makes the two indistinguishable.

The configuration is read once as a plain array, with TypoScriptService::convertTypoScriptArrayToPlainArray and no stdWrap anywhere. So additionalWhere is a static string: a comparison against the current time cannot be expressed in it, and a selection that has to move with the clock is not something this provider can be configured into.

XmlSitemapRenderer builds a provider with makeInstance($class, $request, $sitemapName, $config) — positional arguments, so a provider of your own takes no constructor injection. A service it fetches for itself has to be declared public: true, or makeInstance builds it with no arguments and the request fails with an ArgumentCountError.

Which is what a table whose detail view is not one page needs. The shipped provider fits a table rendered by a single detail page; where several filtered list plugins each answer for part of the table, a provider of your own extending AbstractXmlSitemapDataProvider is what resolves the page per record, and the documentation names the extension point without saying when the shipped one is the wrong tool.

title: What a Record Object Carries, and What Moved Into _system

hints.text: RecordFactory moves the system fields out of a record rather than copying them: extractSystemInformation() reads each one off the raw row and unsets it from the properties. What goes is what TCA[ctrl] declares — crdate, tstamp, sortby, delete, editlock, descriptionColumn, the four enablecolumns (disabled, starttime, endtime, fe_group), the language fields including l10n_state and the diff source, and t3ver_wsid, t3ver_oid, t3ver_state and t3ver_stage. So $record->toArray() holds uid, pid and the record type's own columns, and not one of those.

toArray(true) adds one further key, '_system', holding SystemProperties::toArray(): isDeleted, isDisabled, isLockedForEditing, createdAt, lastUpdatedAt, publishAt, publishUntil, userGroupRestriction, sorting, description, language and version. All twelve are present on every record and each is null where the table declares no such capability, so the key being there says nothing about the table having the field.

The values are the API's rather than the column's. The four dates are \DateTimeImmutable, userGroupRestriction is an int array from GeneralUtility::intExplode() of fe_group and keeps -1 and -2 as they stand, the three is* are booleans, sorting is an int, and language and version are LanguageInfo and VersionInfo objects — toArray() converts one level and leaves those two as they are.

That is what makes the shape dangerous rather than merely different: $row['hidden'] on such an array is absent, not false. An absent key reads as empty, empty reads as not disabled, and a disabled record renders. Nothing throws and nothing is logged, so the wrong value looks like an answer. Read $row['_system']['isDisabled'], or ask the object with $record->getSystemProperties()?->isDisabled().

Record carries getSystemProperties(), getLanguageInfo(), getLanguageId() and getVersionInfo(), and each of them may return null, so the null-safe call is the correct one and not a defensive habit. The full row is still reachable: getRawRecord() hands back the RawRecord the factory was given, whose get() and toArray() carry every column the query selected.

$record->get('hidden') is no fallback either. Record::get() reaches the raw record only where the record has no record type, so the same call returns the raw value on a table without a typeField and throws RecordPropertyNotFoundException on tt_content or pages.

A row therefore reaches a caller in one of two shapes. The plain one — a QueryBuilder fetch, BackendUtility::getRecord(), FormEngine's databaseRow — is flat, with the enable fields at top level under their TCA names; the Record-sourced one has them under _system under the API's names. Code consumed by both reads _system first and falls back to the raw field, because code that reads the field alone is correct on one caller and silently wrong on the other.

pages is the exception. RecordFactory returns a Page for that table, and Page::toArray(true) rebuilds the whole row from the raw record — every selected column, overlaid with the resolved properties, plus _system and the _-prefixed special properties. A page asked that way does carry hidden; Page::toArray() without the argument is the ordinary shape and does not.
Which rows a query returns at all is persistence-reading, and where such objects come from in the frontend is frontend-records.

title: The Title of a Record Detail Page
hints: The <title> of such a detail view is a PageTitleProvider and nothing else. RecordTitleProvider only reports a title that something else has set through setTitle(), and on a page that renders the record itself nothing does — so there is no TypoScript-only way to put a record's title into the head. The provider is a small class listed in config.pageTitleProviders, and it has to be public in Services.yaml.
